taxa.note: The 508-Ma community of British Columbia - the fullest window on Cambrian soft-bodied animals anywhere.
A metre-long apex predator with grasping frontal appendages, first known whole from the Burgess Shale.
A spiny olenellid trilobite that defines the Laurentian faunal province of the Cambrian tropics.
Sponge-grade reef-builders that fringed the Laurentian shelf before vanishing mid-Cambrian.

Laurentia.shared: Burgess-type body plans also occur in South China (Chengjiang) and Gondwana (Emu Bay); the fauna was near-global, the preservation is what is local.

taxa.note: Eel-like jawless chordates whose phosphatic teeth flood Ibex-section limestones and date the rock.
Straight-shelled cephalopods diversifying explosively as the Sauk Sea drowns the craton.
Articulate lamp-shells opening the Ordovician radiation across a clean carbonate seafloor.
A giant straight-shelled nautiloid, metres long, hunting the Ordovician carbonate platform.
Colonial filter-feeders that, with crinoids, carpet the Cincinnatian seafloor of Ohio and Kentucky.
Stalked echinoderm 'sea lilies' at their Ordovician peak on the drowned Laurentian shelf.
Sea scorpions patrolling Silurian lagoons; the Bertie waterlimes of New York preserve them whole.
The 'chain coral', a tabulate that helped build Silurian reefs across the Great Lakes basin.
A few-centimetre forked stem with terminal sporangia - among the first vascular plants to creep onto Laurentia's coasts.
A millipede from Stonehaven in Scotland with open spiracles, among the earliest animals known to have breathed air.
Alum-shale nodules of Sweden preserve millimetre crustaceans in uncrushed three-dimensional phosphate.
A tiny blind agnostid trilobite so widespread it zones the whole Baltic Cambrian.
A large spiny trilobite of the Baltic-Avalonian 'Atlantic' province, unknown on Cambrian Laurentia.

Baltica.shared: Paradoxides marks the cold-water province Baltica shared with Avalonia and Gondwana, distinct from Laurentia's Olenellus fauna - the split that revealed the Iapetus Ocean.

taxa.note: The red 'Orthoceras limestone' of Sweden and Estonia is a graveyard of straight-shelled cephalopods.
Large smooth-shelled trilobites that dominate the Baltoscandian Ordovician platform.
Baltoscandian conodont zones are the global standard for dividing Ordovician time.
Silurian Gotland is a fossilised barrier reef of tabulate and rugose corals and stromatoporoids.
Layered calcareous sponges that built the framework of the Baltic Silurian reefs.
Bony-headed jawless fish appearing in Baltic near-shore sediments as vertebrates take hold.
From Gotland: cord-forming fungal filaments binding soil on bare Silurian ground, before plants had roots.
The Siberian Platform yields the type Tommotian assemblage - the first mineralised skeletons, mostly millimetre tubes and spines.
Siberian archaeocyath reefs are the largest and best-dated of the Early Cambrian world.
An Early Cambrian soft-bodied Lagerstatte in anoxic Siberian shelf muds, older than the Burgess Shale.
Isolated on its own tropical craton, Siberia grows a distinctive Ordovician trilobite fauna.
Colonial tabulate corals build reefs on the warm, isolated Siberian carbonate shelf.
Shelly brachiopod communities of a shelf sea that faced the open Panthalassic ocean.
Solitary and colonial 'horn corals' on Siberian Silurian carbonate banks.
Reef-building sponges continuing the long carbonate history of the isolated craton.
Colonial plankton whose flattened rhabdosomes zone the black shales of Wales and Newfoundland.
A long-spined trilobite of the cool Avalonian shelf, sometimes fossilised in single-file 'conga lines'.
Cool-water brachiopods of a shelf still tied to the Gondwanan margin.

Avalonia.shared: Avalonia's cold-water fauna groups it with Gondwana and Baltica, across the Iapetus from Laurentia.

taxa.note: Single-row graptolites that swarm the Silurian sea as Avalonia collides with Baltica and Laurentia.
A large predatory eurypterid of Welsh Borderland lagoons and near-shore Silurian seas.
Simple forking land plants take root on the newly assembled Avalonian coastline.
A South Australian Lagerstatte where Anomalocaris keeps its compound eyes - tens of thousands of lenses each.
A large redlichiid trilobite typifying the Cambrian shelves of Australia and Antarctica.
Reef sponges fringing the Australian and Transantarctic margins of early Gondwana.
Moroccan mudstones extend Burgess-type soft-bodied preservation into the Ordovician of the Saharan shelf.
A cold-water brachiopod assemblage that spread worldwide as end-Ordovician ice gripped the Saharan pole.
A trilobite of the chilly clastic shelves ringing high-latitude Gondwana.

Gondwana.shared: The Hirnantia fauna is genuinely global - a rare cosmopolitan moment driven by glaciation.

taxa.note: A distinctive low-diversity cold-water shelly province across South America, South Africa and the Falklands.
An index brachiopod of the cool Silurian Malvinokaffric seas, unlike anything in the tropics.
A surprisingly advanced lycophyte from Victoria, Australia - one of the oldest leafy land plants on Earth.
The Bokkeveld Group and Parana Basin preserve the cold-water Devonian brachiopod-trilobite province.
A brachiopod marking the cool southern shelves as the Old Red tropics teemed to the north.
Early sparse vegetation of horsetails and progymnosperms on the southern floodplains.
Cold marine faunas in the seas around a Gondwana buried under Carboniferous ice.
A thick-shelled cold-water bivalve of the peri-glacial Gondwanan seas.
A cold-climate seed plant of the floras that recolonised bare ground as the Karoo ice sheets melted.

Gondwana.shared: The Karoo/Dwyka ice sheet chilled the whole supercontinent; land fossils from this interval are correspondingly scarce.

taxa.note: The tongue-shaped seed-fern leaf that carpets EVERY Gondwanan coalfield - the single most diagnostic fossil of the supercontinent.
A small aquatic reptile of Permian Gondwanan lakes, found on matching shores in Brazil and South Africa - Wegener's evidence for drift.
A tusked herbivorous therapsid abundant across the Karoo before the end-Permian catastrophe.
The whole cool-temperate seed-fern forest - Vertebraria roots, Gangamopteris - that defines Permian Gondwana.
The segmented root of the Glossopteris trees, preserved in Antarctic peat and Indian coal: the plumbing of a forest that grew in polar light.

Gondwana.shared: Glossopteris and Mesosaurus occur right across South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica - the classic shared Gondwanan signature.

taxa.note: A pig-sized dicynodont that survived the extinction and made up most of the Early Triassic Karoo fauna.
A dog-toothed cynodont shared between South American and African Triassic beds.
A forked-frond seed fern that replaces Glossopteris as the dominant Triassic Gondwanan plant.

Gondwana.shared: Lystrosaurus and Cynognathus span South Africa, South America, India and Antarctica - post-extinction faunas were near-cosmopolitan.

taxa.note: An early sauropodomorph from South African Jurassic red beds, known even from embryos in the egg.
One of the earliest true sauropods, from Zimbabwe, as Gondwana begins to break apart.
The Late Jurassic Tanzanian beds preserve Giraffatitan and Kentrosaurus - Africa's answer to the Morrison.
A drought-tolerant conifer family whose pollen swamps Jurassic Gondwanan lowlands. This was the canopy the sauropods fed in.
A Scottish hot-spring deposit that silicified an entire Early Devonian land ecosystem where it stood.
A leafless, rootless forking stem - the textbook early vascular plant, preserved cell-by-cell at Rhynie.
Spider-like arachnids from the Rhynie litter - among the oldest known land predators.
A bony-shielded jawless fish of Old Red Sandstone rivers and lakes.
Eight-metre tapering trunks standing over a knee-high Old Red Sandstone flora. The largest thing alive on land, and a fungus.

Laurussia (Euramerica).shared: Rhynie's plants and arthropods are unique in preservation but the Old Red fauna was shared across Laurussia's rivers from Scotland to Arctic Canada.

taxa.note: The tree of the Gilboa 'forest' in New York - the oldest known forest, of fern-like Wattieza trees.
Giant predatory eurypterids in the near-shore seas of the Old Red continent.
Armoured fish diversifying in Middle Devonian rivers and deltas.
The first modern-looking tree: a real woody trunk, flat leaves and deep roots. Its forests made the first deep soils and pulled down CO2.
A Late Devonian tetrapod from East Greenland with eight-fingered hands - limbs before full land-walking.
An early tetrapod of the Old Red rivers, part fish, part four-legged animal.
An armoured antiarch placoderm so abundant it is the index fossil of Old Red freshwater beds worldwide.
A Scottish Mississippian hot-spring site preserving early terrestrial tetrapods such as Westlothiana.
Scale-tree lycophytes beginning to build the coal swamps that will define the next interval.
Giant predatory lobe-finned fish of the Carboniferous rivers of Laurussia.
A two-metre millipede relative, the largest land arthropod ever, prowling the equatorial coal forests.
A dragonfly-like insect with a 70-cm wingspan, flying in oxygen-rich Carboniferous air.
One of the first true reptiles, sheltering in hollow lycophyte stumps in Nova Scotia.
The dominant scale-tree of the great tropical coal swamps straddling Pangaea's equator.
Strap-leaved coniferophytes thirty metres tall on the drier ground above the coal mires.
The sail-backed synapsid apex predator of the Texas red beds - closer to us than to any dinosaur.
A sail-backed herbivorous pelycosaur sharing the Early Permian floodplains with Dimetrodon.
A heavy-bodied temnospondyl amphibian of the red-bed rivers and swamps.
A boomerang-headed amphibian of Permian ponds, its skull drawn out into broad lateral horns.
The seed fern that marks the Permian red beds across Euramerica: the flora of a continent that had lost its swamps.
Sabre-toothed therapsid predators dominating the late Permian across the whole supercontinent.
Bulky armoured herbivorous reptiles, the cattle of the terminal Permian landscape.
A heavily built pareiasaur from the Russian Permian, knobbly-skulled and barrel-bodied.
The dicynodont that inherited the Earth - after the end-Permian it ranged from Russia to Antarctica.
A slender early theropod dinosaur, hundreds found together at Ghost Ranch in Pangaea's western deserts.
Crocodile-shaped archosaurs lurking in Late Triassic rivers before crocodiles proper existed.
A gracile pack-hunting theropod of the Late Triassic Newark and Chinle basins.
Armoured, pig-snouted herbivorous archosaurs common in northern Triassic red beds.
Flat-headed giant amphibians that mass-died in drying Triassic lakes across Laurasia.
A double-crested early theropod from the Kayenta Formation of the American Southwest.
Small mammal-like cynodonts, herbivorous survivors of the synapsid line into the dinosaur age.
An early armoured dinosaur from the Early Jurassic of England.
The Late Jurassic Morrison Formation - Allosaurus, Stegosaurus, Apatosaurus, Diplodocus - the archetypal dinosaur bonebed.
A high-browsing giant sauropod of the Morrison floodplains of western North America.
The Solnhofen 'first bird', a feathered dinosaur on a Bavarian lagoon at Laurasia's Tethyan edge.
The Hell Creek apex predator of the very end of the Cretaceous, in the last dinosaur ecosystem before the impact.
A three-horned ceratopsian, the commonest large herbivore of latest-Cretaceous western North America.
A duck-billed hadrosaur that grazed the coastal plains beside the retreating Interior Seaway.
A tiny archaic primate relative from just after the K-Pg impact - among the first of our own order.
A sheep-sized archaic hoofed mammal typifying the Paleocene recovery fauna of the western basins.
The 'dawn horse', a dog-sized browser of Eocene woodlands, the base of the classic horse lineage.
A rhino-sized herbivore with six blunt horns and sabre canines from the Bridger Basin.
The herring of the Green River lakes, fossilised by the million in Eocene lake varves.
Dawn-redwood swamp forest ran across the warm Eocene interior and up onto Ellesmere Island, inside the Arctic Circle.
The 'oreodont', a sheep-like cud-chewer so abundant it defines the White River badlands fauna.
A hypercarnivorous creodont, the leading predator of the Oligocene plains.
A huge Y-horned brontothere of the late Eocene-Oligocene grasslands.
A three-toed grazing horse of the spreading Miocene Great Plains grasslands.
A hippo-like short-legged rhino that wallowed in Miocene rivers, mass-buried at Ashfall.
A giraffe-necked camel browsing the tall Miocene savanna of the plains.
The Great Plains grassland spreads through the Miocene, which is why its horses evolve tall, ever-growing teeth.
The American mastodon, a forest browser arriving as Pliocene climate cooled.
A ground sloth from the northward spread of South American mammals via the new Panama land bridge.
The Rancho La Brea sabre-tooth, known from thousands of individuals trapped in asphalt seeps.
The Columbian mammoth, the largest Ice Age grazer of the North American plains.
The dire wolf, the commonest large carnivore in the La Brea tar.
A titanosaur among the largest land animals ever, from the Cretaceous of Patagonia.
A giant carcharodontosaur, rivalling T. rex in size, hunting the Patagonian titanosaurs.
A horned, tiny-armed abelisaur theropod endemic to Cretaceous South America.
A 13-metre snake from the Paleocene Cerrejon rainforest of Colombia - the largest snake known.
A car-sized side-necked turtle sharing Titanoboa's steamy post-impact wetlands.
The oldest neotropical rainforest known: palms, legumes and aroids in a structurally modern canopy only a few million years after the asteroid, and hot enough to support Titanoboa.
An endemic order of South American hoofed mammals that evolved in continental isolation.
Marsupial-relative carnivores that filled the cat-and-dog roles on the island continent.
Endemic hoofed mammals, some convergent on horses and camels, unique to South America.

South America.shared: These endemic orders share the continent with newly rafted-in primates and caviomorph rodents - immigrants that arrived across the Atlantic.

taxa.note: An elephant-like endemic ungulate of the Oligocene Salla and Deseado faunas.
The endemic ungulate radiation continuing through the Oligocene isolation.
A 'terror bird' - a two-metre flightless predator that was a top carnivore of the Miocene pampas.
A giant caiman over ten metres long, ruling the vast Pebas wetland of Miocene Amazonia.
A tapir-like endemic ungulate of the Santa Cruz beds of Patagonia.
Palm-dominated swamp across the Miocene Pebas mega-wetland that filled western Amazonia, the cradle of its modern diversity.
A car-sized armadillo relative in a domed shell, spreading north as the Panama bridge opens.
The sabre-tooth arrives from the north as North and South American faunas mingle in the Great Interchange.

South America.shared: The Great American Interchange makes this interval a two-way mix of endemic southerners and North American immigrants.

taxa.note: A six-tonne ground sloth the size of an elephant - the giant Darwin puzzled over in Patagonia.
A camel-bodied, trunk-nosed litoptern, one of the last of the endemic ungulates.
A glyptodont with a spiked tail-club, among the largest of the armoured Ice Age herbivores.
A sail-backed, semi-aquatic theropod larger than T. rex, from the Kem Kem rivers of the Sahara.
A shark-toothed giant predator of the mid-Cretaceous North African floodplains.
A sail-backed iguanodont sharing the lush Cretaceous river deltas of what is now the desert.
A colossal titanosaur from the mangrove coasts of Late Cretaceous Egypt (Bahariya).
A titanosaur from the East African rift sediments, part of a distinct southern fauna.
A fire- and drought-tolerant tree fern that carpeted the Cretaceous North African floodplains where Spinosaurus and Paralititan lived.
A key early anthropoid from the Fayum of Egypt, near the root of monkeys and apes.
A pig-sized, semi-aquatic early proboscidean - a distant, low-slung ancestor of elephants.
A rhino-like herbivore with two enormous horns, endemic to the Fayum swamps.
Mangrove-palm swamp fringed the Tethyan coast of Africa. The Fayum primates lived in forest right at the water's edge.
An early ape from Miocene East Africa, from the radiation that led to living apes and us.
A large proboscidean with down-curved lower tusks, browsing the Miocene woodlands.
A late-Miocene Chadian hominin near the split of the human and chimpanzee lines.
C4 grasses spread across Africa after about eight million years ago, turning closed woodland into open savanna: the habitat shift that frames human origins.
'Lucy' and her kin - upright-walking hominins of the Pliocene East African savanna.
The Laetoli trackway in Tanzania records these hominins walking bipedally through volcanic ash.
An early tool-making human from Olduvai Gorge, at the base of our own genus.
A robust, massive-jawed hominin ('Nutcracker Man') sharing the Pleistocene rift with early Homo.
Africa keeps the intact big-mammal community - elephants, rhinos, hippos - that other continents lost.
Fungus farmed in gardens inside African termite mounds, an agriculture tens of millions of years older than our own.
An Eocene oil-shale lake in Germany preserving bats, early horses and gut contents in mirror detail.
A small Eocene browsing horse relative, found at Messel with leaves still in its stomach.
A huge flightless bird of the Eocene forests of Europe, once cast as a predator, likely a browser.
Palm fronds and crocodiles at fifty degrees north. Messel preserves a paratropical forest in what is now Germany.
A hornless rhino the size of a small crane - the largest land mammal ever, from the Oligocene of Asia.
'Hell pigs', massive omnivorous artiodactyls of the Oligocene Asian steppes.
A large Miocene ape from the Siwaliks, close to the ancestry of the orangutan.
A three-toed horse whose sudden spread ('the Hipparion datum') marks Miocene Eurasia.
A giant hook-tusked proboscidean ranging the Pikermian savannas of the Miocene.
The woolly mammoth, keystone grazer of the Ice Age mammoth steppe from Iberia to Siberia.
The woolly rhinoceros, its shaggy form known from cave paintings as well as frozen carcasses.
Cold-adapted Eurasian humans who buried their dead and left DNA in most living non-Africans.
The cave bear, whose bones fill Ice Age European caverns by the thousand.
The Ediacara Hills type locality: quilted soft bodies up to a metre across, with cholesterol biomarkers that make Dickinsonia an animal.
A segmented Ediacaran form with a shield-like head end, argued over for decades as a possible early arthropod relative.
Frond-shaped rangeomorphs anchored to the sea floor, feeding without a mouth or a gut.
The lone substantial early-Cenozoic Queensland site (~55 Ma), hinting at South American mammal links, then near silence.
Cool-temperate southern beech rainforest covered Australia before it dried. Its pollen dominates Eocene cores from the coast to the interior.

Australia.shared: After Tingamarra the continent's record goes nearly blank until the Oligocene - the origins of the marsupial groups are poorly constrained here.

taxa.note: A toothed platypus from the Riversleigh limestones, showing the monotreme lineage's deep past.
A sheep-sized tree-dwelling marsupial herbivore, mass-preserved in Riversleigh cave pools.
Early marsupial 'lions' with bolt-cutter premolars appear in the Miocene rainforest fauna.
Eucalypts and charcoal rise together through the Miocene record: fire and increasing aridity remaking a rainforest continent.
The Chinchilla Sand records the Pliocene shift from rainforest to open woodland as Australia dries.
Kangaroos radiate as grasslands spread across the drying interior.
A three-tonne wombat relative, the largest marsupial ever to live.
The marsupial lion, a powerful ambush predator with the strongest bite of any known mammal for its size.
A short-faced giant kangaroo browsing shrubs on one-toed feet.
A seven-metre monitor lizard (Megalania), Australia's largest land predator until the megafauna vanished.
Permian coal and permineralised stumps in the Transantarctic Mountains: forests that grew through six months of polar darkness.
Segmented Glossopteris roots preserved in Antarctic peat, many still standing in growth position.
Southern-conifer forests clothe a warm-temperate Jurassic-Cretaceous Antarctica, still joined to the rest of Gondwana.
Monkey-puzzle relatives form the high-latitude woodland; body-fossils of its animals are scarce in this interval.

Antarctica.shared: Antarctica's most famous dinosaur, the crested Cryolophosaurus, comes from OLDER (~188 Ma) Transantarctic beds just beyond the clickable window; the 100-160 Ma record itself is thin.

taxa.note: The first ankylosaur from Antarctica, from the James Ross Basin of the still-forested Cretaceous continent.
A small ornithopod of the high-latitude Cretaceous forests of the Antarctic Peninsula.
Southern beech - the Seymour Island floras show Eocene Antarctica was cool temperate rainforest, not ice.
A giant penguin, over 1.5 m tall, from the La Meseta beds before the ice arrived.
Marsupials on Seymour Island, recording the old land connection between Antarctica, South America and Australia.

Antarctica.shared: The Nothofagus-marsupial forest links Eocene Antarctica to South America and Australia across Gondwana's last land bridges.

taxa.note: A horned abelisaur theropod from the Lameta beds, hunting amid the erupting Deccan Traps.
A titanosaur of latest-Cretaceous India whose nesting grounds are preserved as fossil egg clutches.
The 'walking whale' of Indo-Pakistani Eocene coasts, a crocodile-like stage in whale origins.
A Vastan lignite mammal near the root of odd-toed ungulates, recording India's brief faunal isolation.
Early bats among the exceptional Eocene mammals of the Cambay lignites as India nears Asia.
Fifty-million-year-old amber from Gujarat holds a dipterocarp rainforest, and insects with Asian relatives: India was already trading life across a narrowing sea.
A great ape of the Siwalik foreland forests shed from the rising Himalaya.
A large proboscidean of the Miocene-Pliocene Siwalik faunas.
The Asian elephant lineage and a rich Siwalik-derived mammal fauna occupy the subcontinent.
Rice-grain foraminifera crowding the Permian carbonate shelves of the Cimmerian blocks.
Spiny brachiopods of the Tethyan Permian margins as the terranes rift from Gondwana.

Cimmeria.shared: The Cimmerian blocks carry a cool-water Gondwanan-derived flora on land, but the fossils that survive are overwhelmingly their marine shelf faunas.

taxa.note: A thin flat 'paper clam' blanketing deep Tethyan Triassic seafloors along the drifting blocks.
Ammonoids with frilled sutures, the standard Triassic timekeepers of the Tethyan shelves.
Recovering conodont faunas zoning the Triassic carbonate ramps of the Cimmerian margin.
A large redlichiid trilobite of the Cambrian carbonate platform of the North China Block.
Early Cambrian reef sponges on the flooded margin of the isolated craton.
The tropical coal-forest flora - Gigantopteris, Lobatannularia - that built the great Shanxi coals.
A large-leaved seed plant diagnostic of the Cathaysian equatorial rainforests of North China.

North China.shared: The Cathaysian flora is shared with South China and Southeast Asian blocks - a distinct equatorial realm separate from Gondwana's Glossopteris and Angara's cold flora.

taxa.note: The Yixian and Jiufotang beds of Liaoning - ash-buried lakes preserving feathers, fur, stomach contents and flowers.
The first dinosaur found with unambiguous filaments, its ginger-and-white banded tail later decoded.
An early beaked bird known from thousands of Jehol specimens, many with long tail streamers.
A four-winged dromaeosaur with flight feathers on all four limbs, glossy black in life.
A badger-sized Jehol mammal found with a juvenile dinosaur in its stomach.
One of the earliest flowering plants known from complete fossils, an aquatic herb in the Yixian lake beds alongside the feathered dinosaurs.
Weng'an phosphorites preserving algae and controversial embryo-like fossils at cellular resolution, ~600 Ma.
Spiny organic-walled microfossils that make the Doushantuo a global Ediacaran reference.
The Yunnan Lagerstatte (~518 Ma), earliest of the great Cambrian faunas, with soft tissues intact.
A Chengjiang fish among the oldest known vertebrates, with gill arches and a notochord.
Another Chengjiang jawless fish, pushing the vertebrate record back to the early Cambrian.
The great predator hunting the Chengjiang seas as it did those of Laurentia.

South China.shared: Chengjiang, the Burgess Shale and Emu Bay share body plans worldwide - the Cambrian fauna was cosmopolitan, its soft-bodied preservation local.

taxa.note: The Meishan section is the global boundary marker for the end-Permian extinction, in continuous marine limestone.
Large foraminifera flourishing on the Lopingian carbonate platform right up to their extinction.
A latest-Permian fusulinid whose disappearance pinpoints the marine mass extinction.
A Middle Triassic marine Lagerstatte in Yunnan documenting the recovery of ocean life after the extinction.
A small long-necked marine reptile found by the thousand in Guizhou Triassic shales.
Dolphin-shaped marine reptiles, including huge Guanling forms, patrolling the Triassic Tethyan shelf.
Layered microbial mounds in shallow-shelf cover sequences - essentially the only fossils the craton preserves here.

Amazonia.shared: Body fossils are absent; the Amazonian craton at this time is basement and thin cover, not a place with a fossil record.

taxa.note: The Tonian Mbuji-Mayi Supergroup yields acritarchs and vase-shaped microfossils - genuine eukaryote fossils from the craton's cover.
Mat-building cyanobacteria and stromatolites of the shallow Tonian shelves on the craton margin.
The Nama Group of Namibia preserves this stack-of-cups tube - among the first animals to build a mineral skeleton.
A goblet-shaped skeletal fossil that, with Cloudina, built the world's first animal reefs.
A quilted, vane-like Ediacaran organism of the terminal-Ediacaran Nama sandflats.
A fractal frondose Ediacaran of the Namibian shelf, type of the whole rangeomorph group.

Kalahari Craton.shared: The Nama assemblage is the flagship terminal-Ediacaran fauna and one of the best records of the dawn of skeletal animals.

taxa.note: Tonian microbial reefs in the carbonate cover; no animals yet in the craton's older rocks.
Testate amoebae from the Chuar Group and elsewhere - the oldest fossils of shelled, predatory eukaryotes.
Organic-walled algal cysts diversifying on the shelves of the supercontinent, abundant enough to date rock.
A filamentous red alga with differentiated cells - among the oldest fossils tied to a living group.
Stromatolite-building cyanobacteria still run the Tonian biosphere across every warm Rodinian shelf.
Chitin-walled branching microfossils from the Arctic shelf of Rodinia, arguably the oldest fungus and older than any animal.

Rodinia.shared: Life everywhere on Rodinia is microbial; nothing is more than millimetres across, and much of the craton interior preserves nothing at all.

taxa.note: Rice-grain foraminifera built reefs on mid-ocean seamounts, now accreted into the rocks of Japan.
Silica-shelled plankton whose ooze became the deep-sea cherts that record this vanished ocean.
Ammonoids swimming the open Panthalassic water above the drowned seamount chains.

Panthalassa.shared: Almost all Panthalassic seafloor has been subducted; what survives is scraped-off seamount caps and radiolarian chert.

taxa.note: A school-bus-sized ichthyosaur from the Panthalassic margin of Nevada, among the largest marine reptiles.
Frill-sutured ammonoids leading the recovery of open-ocean life after the end-Permian collapse.
Radiolarian faunas slowly rebuild the deep-sea plankton through the Triassic.
True ammonites diversify as free-swimming hunters across the Jurassic superocean.
Bullet-shelled squid relatives shoaling in the open Panthalassic water.
Colonial plankton drifting the open Palaeozoic ocean, their remains zoning its black muds.
Jawless chordates whose teeth are the main fossils of this largely subducted ocean.
Silica plankton whose oozes, preserved in rare cherts, are almost all that is left of the ocean floor.

Panthalassic Ocean.shared: Like its successor, this ocean's crust is mostly gone; the plankton preserved on its margins is the record.

taxa.note: The first ammonoids appear and spread through the open Devonian ocean.
Conodont faunas provide the finest timescale for this otherwise fossil-poor ocean.
Pelagic and shelf foraminifera of the Mississippian open ocean and its island arcs.
Radiolarian cherts continue to be the deep-water signature of the ocean.
Trilobites so different on its two shores that the contrast first revealed the ocean's former existence.
Planktic graptolites drifting the widening Iapetus, their zones correlating its opposite margins.
Conodont faunas record distinct warm and cool water masses across the ocean.

Iapetus Ocean.shared: The 'Pacific' (Laurentian) and 'Atlantic' (Baltic-Avalonian) trilobite realms are the classic biogeographic fingerprint of Iapetus.

taxa.note: As Iapetus narrows, once-separate shelly faunas begin to mingle across the closing seaway.
Silurian graptolites of the shrinking ocean before Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia collide.
Planktic graptolites open the record of the Rheic as it widens behind drifting Avalonia.
Cool Gondwanan and warmer northern shelly faunas face each other across the young ocean.
Ammonoids swim the widest Rheic, an ocean now spanning the Devonian tropics.
Tabulate corals and stromatoporoids build reefs on the Rheic's carbonate margins.
Goniatite ammonoids zone the closing Rheic as Gondwana and Laurussia converge in the Variscan collision.
Foraminifera of the last Rheic shelves before the ocean is squeezed out to form Pangaea.
Thick heart-shaped bivalves crowding the Triassic Tethyan carbonate platforms.
Thin flat bivalves blanketing deep Tethyan Triassic seafloors.
Conodonts zone the Tethyan Triassic, then dwindle toward their end-Triassic extinction.
Jurassic ammonites are so widespread and fast-evolving they are the global clock for the period.
Streamlined marine reptiles hunting fish and squid across the warm Tethyan water.
Long-necked marine reptiles patrolling the Tethyan shelves and its Boreal borders.

Tethys Ocean.shared: Jurassic ammonites are genuinely cosmopolitan - the same genera turn up around the whole Tethys and beyond.

taxa.note: Cone- and horn-shaped bivalves that crowd out corals to build the Cretaceous Tethyan reefs.
Planktonic foraminifera radiate through the Tethyan water column, raining shells to the seafloor.
Tiny vase-shaped plankton that zone the Tethyan latest-Jurassic to Early Cretaceous.
Sponge reef-builders framing the Devonian carbonate margins of the older Tethyan ocean.
Early ammonoids swim the Devonian Paleo-Tethys along the northern Gondwanan shelf.
Fusulinid foraminifera flood the Carboniferous carbonate platforms of the Paleo-Tethys.
Crinoidal limestones accumulate on the warm shelves of the ocean.
Permian fusulinids reach their giant, ornate peak, then are annihilated at the end-Permian crisis.
Permian rugose corals of the rich Tethyan reefs as the ocean starts to close behind Cimmeria.
Oxygen-producing mat-builders run the Tonian ocean, raising stromatolite reefs on every warm shelf.
Organic-walled algal cysts are the ocean's plankton - no animals swim it yet.
Red algae are among the few multicellular inhabitants of this microbial sea.

Mirovia.shared: Mirovia is an ocean run entirely by microbes and algae; there are no animals in it anywhere.

taxa.note: Big flat clams littering Cretaceous seafloors, sometimes shells over a metre across.
Keeled planktonic foraminifera raining onto the Cretaceous ocean floor.
Ammonites remain the dominant open-ocean predators until their end-Cretaceous extinction.

Pacific Ocean.shared: Cretaceous planktonic foraminifera and coccolithophores are cosmopolitan - the same plankton fills every ocean of the age.

taxa.note: A serpentine early whale, fully marine at last, cruising the warm Eocene seas.
Diatoms radiate into a dominant plankton group, seeding rich cool-water food webs.
Coin-shaped large foraminifera build carbonate banks on Paleogene tropical shelves.
The largest macropredatory shark ever, hunting whales across the Neogene ocean.
Filter-feeding baleen whales diversify to exploit booming plankton in the cooling seas.
Calcareous nannoplankton continue to floor the ocean with their microscopic plates.
Ammonites of the Hispanic Corridor colonise the narrow young Central Atlantic rift-ocean.
Belemnites spread into the widening seaway between the Americas and Africa.
Giant marine lizards take the top-predator role as the Atlantic widens through the Cretaceous.
Planktonic foraminifera bloom during the anoxic 'black shale' events of the young ocean.
Thin-shelled clams carpet the oxygen-poor Atlantic seafloor of the mid-Cretaceous.

Atlantic Ocean.shared: The Atlantic's Cretaceous plankton is the same cosmopolitan foraminifera-coccolith assemblage seen in every ocean of the age.

taxa.note: Whales become the great predators and grazers of the maturing Atlantic.
Diatoms drive the productive plankton of the cool Cenozoic North Atlantic.
Planktonic foraminifera continue to build deep-sea ooze across the widening basin.
Belemnites shoal in the young ocean opening between drifting India, Madagascar and Antarctica.
Ammonites colonise the widening Cretaceous seaways of the fragmenting southern continents.
Long-necked marine reptiles hunt the new high-latitude waters of the opening ocean.
Coin-sized foraminifera build the Eocene limestones of the Tethyan-Indian shelves as India docks with Asia.
Planktonic foraminifera floor the Paleogene ocean with carbonate ooze.
Reef corals build the rich tropical province of the modern Indian Ocean.
The coelacanth, a living lobe-finned fish, survives in deep refugia off the Comoros.
Dugongs graze the sea-grass meadows of the warm shallow shelves.
Diatoms dominate the plankton of the new circum-Antarctic current, the base of the whole food web.
Antarctic krill swarm on the diatom bloom, feeding whales, seals and penguins.
Icefish evolve antifreeze proteins to fill the freezing waters other fish cannot survive.
Baleen whales migrate in to gorge on the krill of the productive polar sea.

Southern Ocean.shared: The Drake Passage opening (~34-30 Ma) isolates Antarctica and creates this distinctive cold, krill-based ecosystem.

taxa.note: Cold-water foraminifera are the main fossils of the young, often ice-covered polar basin.
Hardy bivalve communities on the shallow Arctic shelves through the Cenozoic.
The bowhead whale, adapted to break sea ice, is the signature large animal of the modern Arctic.

Arctic Ocean.shared: Around 49 Ma a freshwater Azolla fern bloom carpeted a nearly enclosed Arctic - a famous event, but a freshwater one, not part of this marine list.

taxa.note: Coral and mollusc faunas of the warm Miocene sea before it was cut off from the Atlantic.
Reef corals building fringing reefs around the Miocene Mediterranean basin.
After the Messinian salinity crisis dried the basin, salt-tolerant survivors and Atlantic recolonisers rebuild the fauna.
Sea-grass meadows anchor the modern Mediterranean's endemic shelf ecosystem.

Mediterranean.shared: The Messinian Salinity Crisis (~5.96-5.33 Ma) turned the whole sea to salt flats; the modern fauna is a post-flood reassembly.

taxa.note: A mosasaur over twelve metres long, the apex predator of the seaway that split North America.
A ferocious bony fish, sometimes fossilised with an entire swallowed fish inside it.
A four-metre sea turtle, the largest ever, cruising the warm inland sea.
A straight-shelled ammonite so abundant it zones the entire seaway; the chalk records its coccolith plankton.
Spiny trilobites of the transgressive sheet sands drowning the Cambrian Laurentian craton.
The shallow sea records repeated sudden trilobite mass-extinctions and rebounds - the classic 'biomere' pattern.
Clotted microbial mounds build reefs across the vast, nearly flat epicontinental sea.
A ray-finned fish of the Kupferschiefer copper-shale, preserved as the sea first flooded then stagnated.
Spiny brachiopods of the brief carbonate phase before the sea evaporated into thick salt.
Lacy bryozoans forming small reefs on the Zechstein carbonate shelf.

Zechstein Sea.shared: The Zechstein repeatedly dried to halite and potash; its fauna is a low-diversity, stress-tolerant one that came and went with each flooding.

taxa.note: Shallow-shelf foraminifera of the epicontinental seaway that flooded western Siberia for a hundred million years.
Molluscan faunas of the strait that kept European and Asian land mammals apart until it drained.

Turgai Strait.shared: The strait's closure around 29 Ma triggered the 'Grande Coupure' - a wave of faunal exchange as Europe and Asia joined by land.

taxa.note: A giant short-necked pliosaur, apex predator of the cold Cretaceous sea over central Australia.
An ichthyosaur of the Eromanga, some specimens preserved as shimmering opal.
Ammonites of the high-latitude inland sea, their shells among the opalised fossils of Coober Pedy.
An endemic brackish-water mussel that swarmed the isolated, freshening Paratethyan basins.
Cut off from the world ocean, the sea evolved its own peculiar low-salinity mollusc faunas.
Dwarfed, stress-tolerant foraminifera track the sea's swings between marine and near-freshwater.

Paratethys.shared: The Paratethys is the shrunken relic of Tethys; isolation made its fauna strange and endemic, ancestral to the Caspian and Black Sea life of today.

taxa.note: Microbial mats and stromatolites are essentially the only record of an ocean that closed before animals were common.
Sparse organic-walled plankton in the few unmetamorphosed sediments of the vanished ocean.

Mozambique Ocean.shared: This ocean was consumed in the Pan-African/Kuunga collision; its deep-water crust is subducted or metamorphosed, so the record is nearly blank.

taxa.note: On the closing margins of the Adamastor, the Nama and Gariep belts preserve these first skeletal tube-animals.
Microbial reefs dominate the shallow shelves of the ocean before its terminal-Ediacaran skeletal fauna.

Adamastor Ocean.shared: The ocean's Ediacaran shelf record survives on the Kalahari and Congo margins; its deeper floor was destroyed in the Brasiliano collision.

taxa.note: Planktic graptolites of the island-arc seas of the Ordovician-Silurian Ural ocean.
Tabulate corals and brachiopods on the shelves of the ocean between Baltica and Siberia.
Devonian ammonoids and reef faunas along the still-open Uralian seaway.
Reef-building sponges on the Devonian carbonate margins of the ocean.
Fusulinid foraminifera pack the carbonate shelves as the ocean closes in the Uralian orogeny.
The type Permian marine faunas of the Ural foreland - the very rocks the Permian period is named for.

Ural Ocean.shared: The Perm region's marine sections are the global reference for the Permian; the closing Ural Ocean is where they formed.

taxa.note: Drifting graptolites zone the black shales of the seaway separating Baltica from Avalonia.
Distinct Baltic and Avalonian-Gondwanan trilobites on the two shores mark the sea's width.
Cool-water shelly faunas of the shelves flanking the Cambrian-Ordovician seaway.

Tornquist Sea.shared: As Avalonia drifted across the Tornquist Sea to dock with Baltica in the Late Ordovician, the once-separate faunas of the two margins merged.

taxa.note: The first bird — feathered, clawed and toothed — its wings printed in the lagoon's fine limestone.
Long-tailed pterosaur skimming the lagoon; some slabs preserve its wing membrane and throat pouch.
A chicken-sized coelurosaur dinosaur washed into the lagoon, its last meal a lizard in its gut.
A horseshoe crab preserved at the end of its own death-track across the anoxic mud.
Ammonites of the open Tethys, sunk into a stagnant, oxygen-starved basin that let nothing decay.
The ammonoid that zones the whole Muschelkalk — its ribbed shells fill the limestone.
Meadows of stalked crinoids ('sea lilies') whose disarticulated ossicles make crinoidal limestone.
A long-necked, sharp-toothed marine reptile hunting the shallow shelf.
Placodonts — armoured reptiles with flat crushing teeth for shellfish on the sea floor.
The Mowry Shale is paved with fish scales — a bloom-and-death sea of small ray-finned fish.
Silica-shelled plankton so abundant the shale itself is siliceous.
Flat, thick-shelled clams carpeting the early Western Interior seabed.
Bullet-shaped squid relatives swarming the cool northern seas; their guards litter Arctic shales.
Dolphin-shaped reptiles cruising the boreal water column.
Cold-water ammonite faunas distinct from the warm Tethyan realm to the south.
A small clam so abundant and fast-evolving it dates the whole boreal Jurassic-Cretaceous.
Giant marine lizards, the apex predators of the seaway in its final phase.
A flightless, toothed diving bird that swam the seaway like a loon.
Straight-shelled ammonites drifting in vast numbers over the muddy floor.
The 'saber-toothed herring', a fanged predatory fish of the interior sea.
The Bearpaw Shale is a Baculites clock — each zone a different straight-shelled ammonite species.
A large disc-shaped ammonite, some shells punctured by mosasaur tooth-marks.
Mosasaurs patrolling the retreating late-Cretaceous interior sea.
Not a taxon but a legacy: Bearpaw ammonite shells fossilised as the gem ammolite.
Cone- and spiral-shelled bivalves that BUILT the Tethyan reefs where corals had once dominated.
A rich, ornate Tethyan ammonite fauna — the warm-water standard the boreal seas are compared against.
Reef corals of the shallow Tethyan carbonate platforms.
(younger) Coin-sized foraminifera whose shells make the limestone of the Egyptian pyramids.
Giant single-celled foraminifera building whole limestones across the Paleogene Tethys.
Rudist reefs at their peak before collapsing at the end of the Cretaceous.
Star-shaped coccolithophore plankton of the warm Paleogene sea.
Stacked-cone tube-builder, one of the first animals to make a mineralised skeleton — some bored by predators.
A goblet-shaped calcified fossil, an early reef-dweller of the terminal Ediacaran.
A large three-vaned Ediacaran frond of the Nama seafloor, a body plan with no living counterpart.
Fractal, fern-like fronds — the last of the soft Ediacaran biota before the Cambrian.
'Devil's toenails' — thick curved oysters strewn across the Jurassic seabed of western North America.
Belemnite squid whose bullet guards are the commonest Sundance fossil.
Ichthyosaurs hunting the epicontinental sea that reached down from the Arctic.
Stalked crinoids that rafted on driftwood over the open sea.
Lace and twig colonies encrusting the vast, warm Ordovician-Silurian carbonate shelf.
Strophomenid and orthid lamp-shells dominating the shelly benthos.
Solitary 'horn corals' and colonial tabulates building the first big Paleozoic reefs.
Dense crinoid gardens whose broken stems make whole beds of limestone.
Layered sponge-grade reef-builders raising the great Devonian reef complexes.
Spiriferid brachiopods with their broad winged hinges, the Devonian shelf standard.
Armoured fish — including giant Dunkleosteus-kin — the apex predators of the Devonian sea.
Colonial and horn corals flanking the stromatoporoid reefs.
Rice-grain foraminifera so abundant they zone the entire late-Paleozoic cratonic sea.
The 'age of crinoids' — Carboniferous seafloors were forests of stalked echinoderms.
Spiny, one-valve-cemented brachiopods carpeting the shelf.
Bizarre Carboniferous sharks and chimaeras — Helicoprion's tooth-whorl among them.
Caribbean coral reefs before the Isthmus of Panama split them from the Pacific.
Giant megatooth sharks patrolling the warm tropical seaway.
Sea cows grazing sea-grass meadows in the shallow tropical straits.
Larger foraminifera whose divergence across the closing seaway records the Isthmus forming.
A brackish ostracod that boomed as the Mediterranean's chemistry swung wildly during the salinity crisis.
Microbial mats and stromatolites on hypersaline flats as the sea evaporated to gypsum and rock salt.
'Lago Mare' phase — brackish Paratethyan mussels flooding a Mediterranean nearly emptied and freshened before the Atlantic broke back in.
Endemic mussels of the great brackish lake-sea left behind as the Paratethys shrank.
Brackish-water snails that radiated into dozens of endemic Lake Pannon species.
Three-toed horses on the surrounding grassy shores, washed into the lake beds.
Thick clams on the floor of the vast shallow sea flooding the West Siberian basin.
Sharks whose shed teeth are the commonest vertebrate fossil of the epeiric sea.
(younger) Diatom blooms so vast they left the diatomite of the West Siberian basin.
Mosasaurs of the shallow sea that split Africa, known from superb Moroccan and Malian skeletons.
A dazzling shark and ray fauna — the phosphate beds of Morocco are built from their teeth.
(younger) Early whales like Basilosaurus in the warm Eocene straits before the sea withdrew.
Coral reefs of the Coral Triangle — the most biodiverse marine region on Earth today.
Larger reef foraminifera building carbonate sands across the tropical shelf.
The richest reef-fish fauna anywhere, radiating through the young sea.
Whales and dolphins of the cool temperate sea opening between Australia and Zealandia.
Cool-water bryozoan and shell gravels rather than tropical coral — the temperate carbonate style.
The living Nautilus, a survivor of the once-vast shelled-cephalopod dynasties, still haunts these depths.
Rudist bivalves built the great Cretaceous reef rim (the El Abra / Golden Lane banks) around the young Gulf.
Keeled planktonic foraminifera raining onto the deep Gulf floor and into its oil-source chalks.
Ammonites over the open Gulf, ended abruptly by the Chicxulub impact on its own southeastern rim.
Deep-water foraminifera whose ooze became the source rock for the Gulf's vast oil and gas.
Rich molluscan shelf faunas along the subsiding northern Gulf margin.
Megatooth and other large sharks in the warm Neogene Gulf.
Swarming eyeless vent shrimp that dominate Atlantic hydrothermal chimneys, farming bacteria on their shells.
Vent mussels living on sulphur-eating bacteria in their gills — no sunlight, no photosynthesis.
Heat- and sulphur-loving microbes at the base of a food web run entirely on chemistry, not light.
Giant tube worms up to 2 m long, mouthless and gutless, fed by symbiotic bacteria — icons of the 1977 vent discovery.
Big white chemosynthetic clams clustered in the warm sulphide flow around Pacific vents.
The 'Pompeii worm', living on chimney walls in some of the hottest water any animal endures.
Robust ark-clams crowding the sandy floor of the last Paleocene remnant of the interior sea.
Sharks and rays recolonising the epeiric sea after the end-Cretaceous crisis.
Recovering foraminiferal faunas dating the brief Paleocene marine incursion.
Belemnites of the North Sea seaway that let boreal and Tethyan faunas mingle.
Ammonites whose mixing across this strait is how the boreal and Tethyan Jurassic are correlated.
Coiled oysters strewn through the dark organic muds that became North Sea oil shales.
The corridor itself is defined by ammonites — their sudden trans-Pangaean spread marks the seaway opening.
Bivalves dispersing between the eastern Pacific and western Tethys through the narrow tropical strait.

Amazonia.why: Cryogenian-Tonian craton interior: crystalline basement and thin cover with no body fossils - stromatolites at most. The record here is essentially blank.

Congo Craton.why: Cryogenian glacial and craton-interior rocks (Grand Conglomerat and equivalents) carry no animal fossils; only microbial traces survive.
Terminal-Ediacaran cover of the craton is largely unfossiliferous away from the basin margins; no Nama-grade fauna is recorded on the Congo interior itself.

Kalahari Craton.why: Cryogenian snowball interval (Chuos/Ghaub glacials): craton-margin glacial rocks with no animal fossils, only microbial traces. The rich Nama fauna is younger, at the very end of the Ediacaran.

Rodinia.why: Most of the supercontinent's interior is unfossiliferous crystalline rock; the sparse Tonian eukaryote fossils come only from a few marginal basins.

Antarctica.why: Since the ice sheet grew at ~34 Ma the continent has been sealed under kilometres of ice; there is essentially no post-Eocene terrestrial fossil record. The record here is blank, not empty of life.

North China.why: The North China Block stood emergent from the Late Ordovician to the Carboniferous - a ~120-Myr regional unconformity with almost no preserved sediment or fossils.

Panthalassa.why: Most of the superocean's floor has been subducted; away from the rare accreted seamount caps and radiolarian cherts the deep-ocean record is simply gone.

Panthalassic Ocean.why: The Cambrian open ocean off Gondwana and Laurentia is almost entirely subducted; its earliest interval preserves little beyond scattered plankton on former margins.

Mozambique Ocean.why: An ocean that closed in the Pan-African collision: its deep-water crust is subducted or metamorphosed, and it predates abundant skeletonised animals. Little more than microbial traces remains.

Mirovia.why: A Neoproterozoic ocean with no animals - only microbes and algae. There is life, but nothing that leaves a conventional body-fossil record beyond stromatolites and acritarchs.
